author: KTVF11
title: Body of Kotzebue hunter missing since 2025 is found, wife says
text:
The body of a Kotzebue hunter who went missing after falling through sea ice during a hunting trip last fall has been found, according to his wife.
KOTZEBUE, Alaska - The body of a Kotzebue hunter who went missing after falling through sea ice during a hunting trip last fall has been found, according to his wife.
Bergman Pete Nelson Sr., 58, was discovered Sunday by a Kotzebue resident — his nephew Vern — after months of search efforts that stretched through winter conditions, according to his wife Charlotte Nelson. ”It’s a relief, a sigh of relief, like we can finally quit wondering where he is,” she said.
“We can finally put him to rest. ” Nelson had been missing since Nov. 1, 2025, when Alaska State Troopers said three Kotzebue men riding a snowmachine and two four-wheelers went through the ice near Lockhart Point north of Kotzebue. One man made it safely to shore, troopers said.
Another man, 46-year-old Elmer Brown Sr., was rescued from the water but died at a local health clinic that night, according to a Bergman Pete Nelson Sr., 58, was discovered Sunday by a Kotzebue resident — his nephew — after months of search efforts that stretched through winter conditions, according to his wife Charlotte Nelson. Nelson said she learned her husband had been found from her brother while she was in Anchorage.
She said her husband was born and raised in Kotzebue and grew up at camp with his parents, learning traditional ways of living on the land. ”We live in a very modern world now today, and my husband was very high on keeping our tradition and values alive,” she said.
“That’s how he raised our boys to be hunters, just like him and his father and the fathers before them,” she said. “He taught them everything that they needed to survive out there. ” The couple have four children together — Bergman Nelson II, 19; Nicole Nelson, 21; Billy Nelson, 25; and Ariana Nelson, 26. Nelson said they also both have children from other partners.
Nelson said that morning began like many others, with her husband up early and bringing her coffee before leaving to hunt for caribou. She said he had been eager to hunt that weekend before starting seasonal work with a local construction company, and that conditions had been uncertain as weather patterns and ice conditions shifted.
She first learned something had gone wrong through a message from a cousin and later became more alarmed when she tried reaching her husband by phone. She said her family and others gathered at the beach as responders worked. Volunteer searchers from Kotzebue and nearby communities, including Noorvik, continued looking for him even after state efforts were called off.
”The search was called off by the state of Alaska after so many months,” she said, adding that volunteers organized their own efforts and fundraising. Nelson said her husband was known for sharing what he knew about the land and encouraging people to travel safely.
“He would always offer encouragement,” she said. “He always encouraged everybody to know where they’re at, the weather condition, the wind condition, the ice conditions. ” In what now she said feels like somber irony, she reflected on how her husband’s friends gave him the nickname of “Ice,” due to his strong and tough demeanor, with many also calling him “Iceberg.
” “He was just always so ‘get her done’ type of guy, very cold at times because he had that demeanor like his father, just very tough, very stern,” she said. Funeral arrangements are still being finalized, she said, asking people to be patient as the family coordinates travel and logistics.
